title: React Native — Lists, Navigation, Animation & Performance

topics.title: FlatList — how does it work, and how do you make a long list fast?
topics.html:
• ScrollView renders all children immediately. Fine for 10–20 items, fatal for 1000 — it will freeze the app and eat memory.
  • FlatList is virtualized: it only renders a window of items around the visible area and unmounts the rest. That is the whole point of using it.
  • The window is controlled by props, and knowing these names is exactly what an interviewer is checking:
PropWhat it does
keyExtractorStable identity per row. Use the item id, never the index.
getItemLayoutTells the list each row's height up front, so it can skip measuring. Big win — only possible for fixed-height rows.
initialNumToRenderHow many rows to render on the first paint. Keep it to roughly one screen.
maxToRenderPerBatch / updateCellsBatchingPeriodHow much work per batch while scrolling. Lower = smoother scroll, more blank space.
windowSizeHow many screens' worth to keep mounted around the viewport. Default 21 (10 above, 10 below).
removeClippedSubviewsDetaches off-screen views natively. Helps on Android, can cause blank rows — test it.
onEndReached + onEndReachedThresholdInfinite scroll / pagination.
const renderItem = useCallback(
  ({ item }: { item: Row }) => <Item row={item} onPress={onPress} />,
  [onPress]
);

const Item = memo(function Item({ row, onPress }: ItemProps) {
  return (
    <Pressable onPress={() => onPress(row.id)} style={styles.row}>
      <Text numberOfLines={1}>{row.title}</Text>
    </Pressable>
  );
});

<FlatList
  data={rows}
  renderItem={renderItem}
  keyExtractor={(item) => item.id}
  getItemLayout={(_, index) => ({ length: ROW_H, offset: ROW_H * index, index })}
  initialNumToRender={10}
  windowSize={7}
  onEndReachedThreshold={0.5}
  onEndReached={loadMore}
/>
  • Make the row component cheap. Wrap it in memo, keep renderItem stable with useCallback, and do not create inline objects or arrow functions inside the row if you can avoid it.
  • FlashList (Shopify) is the common upgrade. It recycles views instead of unmounting and remounting them, which is why it stays smooth with complex rows. Drop-in API, and v2 removes the old estimatedItemSize requirement.
  • Never nest a FlatList inside a ScrollView in the same direction — you get the "VirtualizedLists should never be nested" warning and lose virtualization entirely. Use ListHeaderComponent / ListFooterComponent instead.
  • SectionList for grouped data with sticky headers. Same virtualization, same props.
💬 Say it like this

A ScrollView renders everything at once, so for any real list I use FlatList, which is virtualized — it keeps only a window of rows mounted around the visible area.

To make it fast I do three things. First, stable keys from the item id. Second, make the row cheap: memoize the row component and keep renderItem stable, otherwise every scroll re-renders every visible row. Third, if the rows are a fixed height I give it getItemLayout so it does not have to measure anything. If the rows are complex I move to FlashList, because it recycles views instead of mounting new ones.

And one rule I never break: no FlatList inside a ScrollView — that silently turns virtualization off.

Why do I see blank cells when scrolling fast?
The JS thread cannot render new rows fast enough. Fix the row cost first, then tune windowSize and maxToRenderPerBatch, add getItemLayout, and consider FlashList. A placeholder row makes the gap look intentional.
What happens if you use the index as a key?
Same problem as on the web: deleting or reordering items makes React reuse the wrong row, so state, inputs and animations jump to the wrong item.
How do you implement pull to refresh?
refreshing + onRefresh props, or a RefreshControl. Keep the refreshing flag tied to the request state, not to a timer.

topics.title: Navigation — how does it work and what are the traps?
topics.html:
• React Navigation is the default choice. native-stack uses the real native navigators (via react-native-screens), so transitions and gestures feel native. The older JS stack is customisable but slower.
  • Navigator types: Stack (push/pop screens), Tabs, Drawer, and nesting them — a stack inside each tab is the standard app shape.
  • Expo Router is file-based navigation built on React Navigation: a file in app/ is a route, like Next.js. Same concepts underneath.
  • Alternative: react-native-navigation (Wix) is fully native — faster in theory, much smaller ecosystem in practice.

The traps interviewers ask about:

  • Screens stay mounted. Going from A to B does not unmount A. So useEffect(..., []) does not run again when you come back. Use useFocusEffect or useIsFocused for "run when this screen is shown".
  • Params must be serializable. Do not pass functions, class instances or whole objects. Pass an id and read the data from your store or cache. Non-serializable params break state persistence and deep links.
  • Deep linking needs a linking config that maps URLs to screens, plus native setup: URL scheme and Universal Links on iOS (apple-app-site-association), intent filters and App Links on Android (assetlinks.json).
  • Android back button is handled by the navigator, but for custom behaviour — closing a modal, a confirm-on-exit dialog — you hook BackHandler and return true to say "I handled it".
  • Auth flow: do not push the login screen on top. Render a completely different navigator based on auth state, so there is no way to swipe back into the app.
// "run every time this screen is focused, clean up when it is not"
useFocusEffect(
  useCallback(() => {
    const sub = startListening();
    return () => sub.remove();
  }, [])
);

// pass an id, not the object
navigation.navigate("Details", { id: item.id });
💬 Say it like this

I use React Navigation with the native stack, because it uses the real platform navigators so gestures and transitions feel right.

The thing that surprises people coming from the web is that screens are not unmounted when you navigate away — they stay in the stack. So an effect with an empty dependency array will not re-run when the user comes back, and I use useFocusEffect for anything that should happen on focus, like refreshing data.

The other rule is that route params must be serializable — I pass an id and read the entity from the cache, never the object or a callback.

How do you navigate from outside a component, e.g. from an API error handler?
A navigation ref created with createNavigationContainerRef and passed to the container, then navigationRef.navigate(...). Keep it for rare cases like auth expiry; normal navigation goes through the hook.
navigate vs push vs replace?
navigate goes to an existing screen if it is already in the stack; push always adds a new copy; replace swaps the current screen so back does not return to it — the usual choice after login.
Why does my screen flicker or lose state on Android rotation?
Usually the activity being recreated, or heavy work in the focus effect. Check configChanges in the manifest and move expensive work out of focus handlers.

topics.title: Animations — Animated vs Reanimated, and what useNativeDriver really does.
topics.html:
Animated (built in)Reanimated 3/4
Where it runsJS thread by default; UI thread with useNativeDriver: trueUI thread, always, through JSI worklets
What can be animated nativelyOnly transform and opacity (plus colors in newer versions)Any style property, including layout
GesturesPanResponder, on the JS threadreact-native-gesture-handler, on the UI thread
Good forSimple fades, slides, a one-off transitionAnything gesture-driven, complex, or that must never drop a frame
  • useNativeDriver: true sends the whole animation description to native once, then the UI thread plays it frame by frame without asking JavaScript. That is why it keeps running smoothly even while the JS thread is busy.
  • It cannot animate layout properties like width, height, top or margin, because those require a layout pass. Animate transform: [{ scale }] or translateX instead — and if you truly need width, expect it to run on the JS thread.
  • Reanimated uses "worklets": small JS functions marked "worklet" that are compiled to run on the UI thread. useSharedValue holds the animated value, useAnimatedStyle maps it to styles, and runOnJS is how you call back into normal JS.
  • LayoutAnimation animates the next layout change automatically — cheap and easy for list insert/remove, but limited and needs a flag to be enabled on Android.
  • InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions delays heavy work until the current animation finishes. Useful, but it is a scheduling tool, not an optimisation.
// Reanimated: this whole animation lives on the UI thread
const offset = useSharedValue(0);

const style = useAnimatedStyle(() => ({
  transform: [{ translateX: offset.value }],
}));

const gesture = Gesture.Pan()
  .onChange((e) => { offset.value += e.changeX; })
  .onEnd(() => { offset.value = withSpring(0); });

<GestureDetector gesture={gesture}>
  <Animated.View style={[styles.card, style]} />
</GestureDetector>
💬 Say it like this

The built-in Animated API runs the animation on the JS thread by default, which means if React is busy rendering, the animation stutters. Turning on useNativeDriver hands the whole animation to the native side once, so it plays on the UI thread — but that only works for transform and opacity, because anything that changes layout needs a layout pass.

For anything gesture-driven I use Reanimated with gesture-handler. Reanimated compiles small functions called worklets that actually execute on the UI thread, so dragging a sheet or a swipeable row stays at 60 FPS even if the JS thread is doing work. That is the main reason it is the standard choice in production apps.

Why is my animation smooth in release but janky in debug?
Dev mode has no optimisations, plus dev tooling and console logs load the JS thread. Never judge performance from a debug build.
What is runOnJS for?
Worklets run in a separate UI-thread context, so they cannot call normal JS functions directly. runOnJS(setState)(value) bridges back — for example to update React state when a gesture ends.
Pressable vs TouchableOpacity?
Pressable is the modern one: press states, hitSlop, long press, and Android ripple in one API. Touchables are legacy but still everywhere in older code.

topics.title: Images and assets — the quiet cause of most memory problems.
topics.html:
• Local images use require("./logo.png") with a static, literal path — the bundler resolves it at build time, so you cannot build the path from a variable.
  • Resolution suffixes are automatic: logo.png, logo@2x.png, logo@3x.png. The right one is picked per device.
  • Remote images need explicit width and height, or they render with zero size. A local require knows its own dimensions; a URL does not.
  • The real trap: a 4000×3000 photo is decoded into memory at full size even if it is displayed in a 100×100 avatar. A list of those will crash a low-end Android device. Resize on the server or via a CDN, and request the size you actually display.
  • resizeMode: cover / contain / stretch / center — same idea as object-fit.
  • expo-image (or FastImage in older projects) adds proper disk caching, placeholders, blurhash and smoother transitions. Plain Image caching is basic.
  • SVG is not supported natively — you need react-native-svg.
💬 Say it like this

Images are where memory problems usually come from. The image is decoded at its full original resolution in memory, not at the size on screen, so a list of full-size photos in small avatars will crash cheap Android phones. So I always make sure the server or CDN gives me an image close to the display size.

The other two practical things: remote images need explicit width and height or they simply do not appear, and for anything list-heavy I use expo-image because it has real disk caching and placeholders.

How do you load an image whose path is dynamic?
You cannot require a variable. Either use a map object of static requires, or serve it as a URL.
How do you keep app size down?
Ship WebP instead of PNG, avoid bundling large assets that could be downloaded, enable R8/Proguard on Android, use an Android App Bundle so Google Play ships per-device variants, and check what native SDKs actually cost you.

topics.title: "The app feels slow." Walk me through how you debug it.
topics.html:
Give this as an ordered process, not a list of tricks. That is what separates a senior answer.

  • 1. Reproduce on a release build, on a real low-end Android device. Debug builds are 2–10× slower and prove nothing.
  • 2. Find which thread is dropping frames with the Perf Monitor. JS thread → your React code. UI thread → views and images. (See the threads card.)
  • 3. If it is the JS thread: open the React DevTools Profiler and find what re-renders. The usual suspects — a context value that changes every render, an inline object or arrow passed to a memoized child, a store selector returning a new array each time, state that lives too high in the tree.
  • 4. If it is a list: apply the FlatList checklist — memoized rows, stable renderItem, getItemLayout, or FlashList.
  • 5. If it is the UI thread: look at image sizes, the depth of the view tree, shadows and blurs on Android, and any synchronous native work.
  • 6. Startup time: measure TTI. Fixes are lazy-loading screens, not importing heavy libraries at the root, deferring non-critical work with InteractionManager, and confirming Hermes is on.
  • 7. Confirm with numbers. Before/after frame drops, TTI, or a profiler trace — not "it feels better now".
Also worth saying: "console.log in a release build is not free — every log crosses to native. I strip them with babel-plugin-transform-remove-console."
💬 Say it like this

First I reproduce it on a release build on a cheap Android phone, because debug numbers are meaningless. Then I open the Perf Monitor to see whether the JS thread or the UI thread is dropping frames, because the fix is completely different.

If it is JS, I profile with React DevTools and look for unnecessary re-renders — usually a context or a selector handing out a new reference every render. If it is a list, I go through the FlatList checklist: memoized rows, stable renderItem, fixed row height. If it is the UI thread, it is almost always oversized images or a very deep view tree.

And I always finish by measuring again, so I can say what actually changed instead of guessing.

Which tools do you use?
RN DevTools (the built-in debugger since 0.76, replacing Flipper), React DevTools Profiler, the Perf Monitor overlay, the Hermes sampling profiler, and for deep native work Android Studio Profiler or Xcode Instruments.
What is the single most common cause you see?
Unnecessary re-renders of list rows, caused by a new function or object identity being passed down every render.
Does the New Architecture fix performance by itself?
It improves startup and rendering overhead, but it does not fix bad renders or huge images. Architecture removes a ceiling; it does not remove your own work.

topics.title: Layout and UI traps — the ones that catch every React Native beginner.
topics.html:
• Text outside <Text> — a bare string inside a View throws. Every character on screen lives in a Text.
  • flex: 1 does nothing — the parent has no height. You need an unbroken chain of flex: 1 down from the screen root.
  • Percentage height inside an auto-height parent — height: "50%" needs a parent with a real height, exactly like CSS.
  • overflow: "hidden" is unreliable on Android for transformed or elevated children. Test it on both platforms, never only on the simulator.
  • zIndex is not enough on Android — add elevation, and remember elevation also draws a shadow.
  • Shadows differ — iOS uses shadow* props, Android uses elevation. A "shadow" that works on iOS and looks flat on Android is the classic bug.
  • SafeAreaView is iOS-only and does not handle Android notches or gesture bars. Use react-native-safe-area-context with useSafeAreaInsets().
  • Text is clipped or cut off on Android — Android adds font padding and handles line height differently. Use numberOfLines deliberately, and avoid fixing text height in pixels.
  • Tiny tap targets — an icon of 16 px is not tappable. Use hitSlop and aim for about 44×44 of touchable area.
  • Nothing is tappable inside a parent with position: "absolute" that overflows its parent on Android — the part outside the parent bounds does not receive touches.
  • ScrollView with a long list — always FlatList once the data can grow.
  • KeyboardAvoidingView behaves differently per platform — behavior="padding" on iOS, usually "height" or nothing on Android, where windowSoftInputMode in the manifest does the work.
  • First tap on a button while the keyboard is open only dismisses the keyboard — set keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled" on the ScrollView.
💬 Say it like this

Most of the surprises come from assuming CSS rules apply. There is no cascade, flex: 1 only works when the parent has a height, overflow: hidden and zIndex behave differently on Android where you need elevation, and shadows are two completely different APIs per platform.

The other big group is touch and keyboard: small icons need hitSlop, anything absolutely positioned outside its parent stops being tappable on Android, and the keyboard needs keyboardShouldPersistTaps or the user's first tap is eaten. These are the things I check on a real Android device before I call a screen done.

Why does it look right on the iOS simulator and wrong on a real Android phone?
Different font metrics, different pixel densities, notches and gesture bars, and simulators have far more CPU and memory than a budget phone. Test on a real low-end Android device — that is where every problem appears first.

topics.title: Behaviour and lifecycle traps — the ones that only show up in production.
topics.html:
• Screens do not unmount on navigate. Effects with [] do not re-run. Use useFocusEffect. Also means timers and subscriptions on a "closed" screen keep running if you forgot to clean up.
  • App state changes. The app can be backgrounded at any moment. Use AppState to pause polling, refresh stale data on return, and re-check auth. On Android the OS can kill the process entirely and restore it later.
  • Timers keep firing after unmount. Always clear setInterval / setTimeout and remove listeners in the effect cleanup — otherwise you get "state update on an unmounted component" and a real memory leak.
  • No network is a normal state, not an edge case. Mobile connections drop constantly. Handle timeouts, retries, and "we are offline" UI explicitly — a spinner that never ends is the most common mobile bug.
  • Permissions can be denied forever. Handle "denied", "never ask again" and "restricted", and offer a link to system Settings. Ask at the moment the feature is used, not at startup.
  • Android back button — needs BackHandler for custom behaviour. There is no equivalent on iOS, so do not design a flow that depends on it.
  • Deep links can open your app at any screen, including when the user is logged out. The entry state must be handled.
  • Dev vs release differences: __DEV__-only code, remote debugging changing timing, and logs slowing the JS thread. Always verify a bug in a release build before chasing it.
  • Third-party library does not support the New Architecture — this is the number one reason upgrades stall. Check compatibility before adding a dependency.
  • iOS and Android date/number formatting differ if you rely on locale defaults. Pin the locale and format explicitly.
  • Secrets in the JS bundle are not secret. Anyone can unzip an APK and read the bundle. API keys belong on your backend.
💬 Say it like this

The traps that hurt in production are about lifecycle rather than layout. Screens stay mounted, so cleanup matters much more than on the web — an interval left running on a screen the user "left" will keep firing and draining battery.

Then there is the mobile reality: the app can be backgrounded or killed at any time, the network disappears in a lift, permissions can be permanently denied, and a deep link can drop the user into any screen while logged out. I treat all of those as normal states with real UI, not as edge cases.

How do you handle an app that was killed and restored?
Persist the minimum needed state (auth token in secure storage, draft input), let the navigator restore its state, and re-fetch rather than trusting stale cached data.
What do you do when a user reports a bug you cannot reproduce?
Crash reporting with source maps (Sentry/Crashlytics), breadcrumbs for the last actions, device and OS version in the report, and a feature flag to turn the suspect feature off without waiting for a store release.
